result: Single-cell RNA sequencing of PBN tissue from 10 mice identified 21 neuronal subclusters (N1-N21) among 39,649 cells, with neurons comprising 57.2% of cells. The dataset achieved high quality metrics (median 47,177 reads/cell, 1740 genes/cell) and identified major cell types including oligodendrocytes (24.1%), astrocytes (8.1%), microglia (2.6%), and stromal cells. High-resolution neuronal analysis of 7635 neurons (99,583 reads/cell) revealed 19 glutamatergic subclusters (N1-N19, with 90% expressing Slc17a6/Vglut2) and 2 GABAergic subclusters (N20-N21).
evaluation: The scRNA-Seq methodology is well-described with appropriate quality control metrics (C29-C31, C41). The identification of 21 neuronal subclusters is supported by clustering analysis with clear quantification of cell type proportions (C32-C40, C42-C45). The high sequencing depth and gene detection rates provide confidence in the results. The large number of oligodendrocytes is appropriately explained by the anatomical structure (C36).

result: Transcription factor analysis revealed two major neuronal clades: an Atoh1-descendant clade (N4-N12) expressing Lhx2, Lhx9, Meis2, and Nrf1 that projects via the ventral pathway, and an Lmx1-expressing clade (N13-N18) expressing Lmx1a/b, Pou2f2, Pou6f2, En1, Tlx3, Onecut2, and Satb2 that projects via the central tegmental tract. These clades are largely non-overlapping and have distinct projection patterns. Additional subclusters (N1-N2 expressing Slc17a7, N20-N21 GABAergic) show distinct transcription factor profiles.
evaluation: The transcription factor-based classification is well-supported by the scRNA-Seq data (C46-C49, C52-C53) and validated by cited developmental studies (C48, C50). The association between transcription factor expression and projection patterns (C51) is supported by both current data and prior literature. The identification of novel subclusters alongside known populations (C57-C58) demonstrates the increased resolution of this analysis.

result: Neuropeptide and GPCR expression analysis revealed that some neuropeptides (Calca, Ghrh, Nps, Npy, Pdyn, Pnoc) are restricted to one or two subclusters, while others (Adcyap1, Cck, Crh, Gal, Nmb, Nts, Penk, Tac1, Vgf) are expressed across multiple subclusters. GPCRs show generally lower expression than neuropeptides, making scRNA-Seq particularly valuable for their detection and providing potential therapeutic targets.
evaluation: The neuropeptide expression patterns are clearly documented in the data (C59-C60) with appropriate reference to supplementary tables. The utility of GPCR identification for circuit mapping (C61) and therapeutic targeting (C62) is appropriately framed as potential applications. The technical challenge of detecting low-abundance GPCRs (C63) and the value of scRNA-Seq for this purpose (C64) are well-justified.

result: Multiplexed in situ hybridization (HiPlex) across five Bregma levels (−5.0 to −5.4 mm) validated the anatomical localization of neuronal subclusters. Of 19 glutamatergic subclusters, 13 (N4, N7-N17, N19) were localized within the PBN proper, while others were in adjacent regions (N1-N3) or could not be identified (N5, N6, N18). GABAergic neurons (N20-N21) were sparsely scattered throughout the PBN. Each subcluster typically showed prominent expression in one subregion with scattered cells in other regions.
evaluation: The HiPlex methodology is clearly described (C65-C67, C70) with appropriate anatomical reference to the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas. The identification of 13 glutamatergic subclusters within PBN proper (C68, C73) is supported by the imaging data, with honest acknowledgment of subclusters that could not be localized (C72). The data are made publicly available (C69), enhancing reproducibility. The supplementation with RNAScope (C71) provides additional validation.

result: Viral tracing using AAV1-DIO-YFP and AAV1-DIO-synaptophysin:mCherry in 21 Cre-driver lines (4-5 mice per line) revealed brain-wide projection patterns. PBN neurons project via two major ascending pathways: the central tegmental tract (CTT) from PBle neurons and the ventral pathway (VP) from dorsal PBN neurons (PBld/ls/lc). Additional minor pathways include a periventricular pathway through the PAG and a weak descending pathway to the hindbrain.
evaluation: The viral tracing methodology is well-described (C75-C77) with appropriate sample sizes and validation against in situ hybridization (C78). The identification of two major projection pathways (C80-C82) is supported by both current data and cited literature. The description of minor pathways (C83-C84) and the observation that no lines project exclusively along these pathways (C85) demonstrates thorough characterization. The functional relevance of specific projections (C86) is appropriately cited.

result: Detailed projection mapping revealed that PBle neurons primarily target the BNST (oval/ventral regions) and CEA (capsular region), with secondary targets including IC, SI, VPMpc, and PSTN. Dorsal PBN neurons target ventral brain regions (VTA, LHA, DMH, PVH, MEPO). Specific populations show distinct projection patterns: Satb2 neurons project around (rather than into) the core BNST/CEA regions targeted by Calca neurons, while Ntsr1 neurons specifically target the VMH. PBmm neurons do not show a separate innervation profile.
evaluation: The projection mapping is comprehensive with clear identification of primary (C87-C88) and secondary (C90-C92) targets. The consistency across PBle-expressing lines (C91) strengthens the conclusions. The distinction between dorsal and ventral projection patterns (C93-C95) is well-documented. The specific examples of Satb2 (C98-C100) and Ntsr1 (C101-C104) neurons demonstrate the resolution of the approach, with appropriate citation of prior work identifying VMH-projecting neurons (C102). The conclusion about PBmm neurons (C96-C97) is appropriately cautious given the lack of exclusive markers.

result: The study acknowledges multiple technical limitations: widespread gene expression in regions surrounding PBN made restricting viral transduction challenging; GABAergic neurons were too sparse to determine their projection patterns; sequencing depth (~100,000 reads/neuron) may have been insufficient to detect rare transcripts (e.g., Oprm1); some HiPlex probes failed to produce detectable signals; only male mice were used for HiPlex experiments; and the rostral-most PBN region was not included in HiPlex analysis.
evaluation: The authors provide an honest and thorough assessment of limitations. The technical challenges with viral transduction (C105, C140-C141) and GABAergic neuron characterization (C106-C107) are clearly stated. The discrepancy between scRNA-Seq and Cre-driver line expression (C129) is appropriately interpreted as a detection limitation. The failure of some HiPlex probes (C137-C138) and incomplete anatomical coverage (C143) are acknowledged. The lack of sex as a variable (C135) and potential batch effects (C142) are noted. These limitations do not invalidate the main findings but appropriately contextualize them.

result: The PBN is a major hub located at the midbrain-pons junction that receives diverse sensory information from internal organs (via vagus-NTS pathway), pain/temperature signals (via spinal cord and trigeminal pathways), taste (via NTS), and blood-borne signals (via area postrema). The PBN is primarily glutamatergic with abundant neuropeptide expression and projects to multiple forebrain regions including PAG, extended amygdala, cortex, thalamus, and hypothalamus. It plays critical roles in taste, pain, temperature, breathing, cardiovascular control, arousal, and homeostasis.
evaluation: These claims represent well-established knowledge about PBN anatomy and function, appropriately cited from prior literature (C8-C9, C15, C17, C22, C26-C27). The anatomical descriptions (C6, C23-C26) and functional roles (C1-C2, C21-C22) provide essential context for the study. The characterization of inputs (C10-C19) and outputs (C20) is based on extensive prior work. This background information is accurate and appropriately referenced.

result: The study provides a comprehensive molecular and anatomical characterization of PBN neurons at higher resolution than previously achieved, revealing that most PBN neurons express multiple neuropeptides and GPCRs. The results are consistent with prior immunohistochemistry studies and a new spatial-profiling method (PixelSeq). The dataset provides a baseline for future studies examining PBN development and responses to environmental challenges, though additional work is needed to determine whether closely related clusters have distinct functions.
evaluation: The summary statements appropriately contextualize the findings within prior work (C112-C113, C115-C116, C118) and acknowledge the increased resolution achieved (C120). The observation that most neurons express multiple neuropeptides/GPCRs (C110) is supported by the data. The validation by independent methods (C118) strengthens confidence in the results. The identification of future research directions (C108, C114, C121) is appropriate. The discussion of GABAergic neurons (C123-C126) appropriately cites prior work and includes unpublished validation data.

result: The study discusses experimental approaches using Cre-driver lines, noting that both restricted and widespread expression strategies have limitations because threats rarely activate single cell types and activation of some PBN neurons can suppress others. Alternative approaches like FosTrap may address these limitations. The study provides a comprehensive resource including scRNA-Seq data, HiPlex images, and projection maps from 21 Cre-driver lines, all publicly available, with most mouse lines deposited at Jackson Laboratory.
evaluation: The critical evaluation of Cre-driver line approaches (C146-C153) demonstrates sophisticated understanding of experimental limitations, appropriately citing prior work. The suggestion of alternative approaches (C154) is well-justified. The summary of projection pathway characterization (C155-C163) appropriately integrates historical and recent work. The discussion of ongoing input mapping efforts (C164-C165) and the utility of the current dataset (C166) is appropriate. The emphasis on data availability (C169-C170) and resource sharing enhances the impact of the work (C167-C168, C171).
